To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the spatial pattern of Scots pines, black alders, common oaks and common birches in uneven-aged Scots pine dominated forest was random at the beginning of forest succession, and it shifted toward clumped or uniform pattern during the 14-year period.
the spatial patterns of trees in uneven-aged forest change with forest development and that the changes in spatial structure are species-specific.

the spatial patterns of tree species and interspecific associations between them in uneven-aged Scots pine forest are complex and species-specific, and they do not change significantly over 14-year forest development.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the spatial structure of uneven-aged Scots pine forest.
the complexity of natural uneven-aged forests, which results from the heterogenic structure of their components, reflected among others in the spatial pattern of trees.
the spatial structure and dynamics of the uneven-aged forest.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the spatial structure of the uneven-aged Scots Pine forest was not random and that the spatial patterns of individual tree components were species-specific.
the forest structure is not static but dynamic.
species-specific spatial pattern of uneven-aged forest is an important factor determining the forest development and species coexistence.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the spatial pattern of the studied forest is a result of the interaction of different ecological processes operating at different spatial scales.

the spatial pattern of the uneven-aged Scots pinewood forest is species-specific and it is a result of the interaction between species-specific mortality and the species-specific ecological requirements.

the complexity of uneven-aged forest structure is a result of the spatial pattern of trees, which is a consequence of the spatial interactions between individuals and the species-specific ecological requirements.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the forest structure is not static, but it changes over time, which is reflected in the spatial patterns of tree species and their interspecific interactions.
spatial structure of forest is not a static phenomenon, and it should be monitored and analyzed over time.
the spatial structure of uneven-aged forests can be used as an indicator of their health and as a tool for forest management.
